rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: They place the lote tree in the seventh Heaven, to the right of the Divine Throne; it marks Paradise’s end or the limit of creation beyond which none passes or knows.
rows.anchor: Most say it is a tree in the seventh Heaven to the right of the Divine Throne

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: Another view places the lote tree between the sixth and seventh heavens and takes the Garden of refuge as the seventh Heaven.
rows.anchor: Others say the lote tree is at the boundary between the sixth and seventh heavens (Ṭū). In this interpretation, the Garden of the refuge is taken as a reference to the seventh Heaven

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden of refuge is also said to be where the spirits of prophets, the righteous, and witnesses take refuge.
rows.anchor: It is said to be the Garden in which the spirits of the prophets, the righteous, and those who bear witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s gaze did not turn away from the wonders being revealed to him.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s gaze did not swerve from the wonders being revealed to him (Aj).

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: More generally, the verse means the Prophet did not turn away from the truth he sought.
rows.anchor: More generally, it implies that he did not swerve away from the truth that he sought (Ṭū).

rows.speaker: Ṭū
rows.claim: He did not seek anything beyond what was disclosed, whether the vision was of Gabriel or God.
rows.anchor: Nor did it transgress then means that he did not seek anything beyond what was disclosed to him (Ṭū), whether it was the vision of Gabriel or the vision of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that disbelievers look only to worldly matters and are ignorant of religion.
rows.anchor: The extent of their knowledge can be seen as a reference to the fact that the disbelievers look only to the world and are ignorant of religion (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, their claims about angels and idols rest only on conjecture, caprice, and desire.
rows.anchor: or as an indication that their “knowledge,” especially as pertains to the angels and idols mentioned in the preceding verses, derives solely from conjecture, caprice, and their own desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second sentence recurs in 6:117, appears with minor variation in 68:7, and is also compared with 28:85.
rows.anchor: The second sentence of this verse is repeated in 6:117, and with minor variation in 68:7 (see also 28:85).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Generally, the statement means God knows the final ends of all things.
rows.anchor: In general it indicates that God knows the final ends of all things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, God knows the difference between Muslim and pagan beliefs.
rows.anchor: in this context it also refers to God knowing the difference between the beliefs of the Muslims and that of the pagans.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akdā derives from al-kudyah, hard rock encountered while digging; the verb can mean that a well digger hit rock.
rows.anchor: Withheld translates akdā, which derives from

rows.speaker: the Arabs
rows.claim: Arabs used the phrase for digging a well and striking hard rock.
rows.anchor: the Arabs say, “He dug and came upon hard rock

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akdā becomes a metaphor for any endeavor that fails.
rows.anchor: The verb akdā is then used as a metaphor for any endeavor that fails

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who think past deeds suffice or consider themselves pure and stop doing good may find even earlier deeds come to nothing.
rows.anchor: when people are satisfied that past deeds will suffice or consider themselves pure and consequently cease to perform good deeds, even past deeds may come to naught.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like an unproductive well, an endeavor is useless if one digs but never reaches water.
rows.anchor: Similarly, the effort to dig a well is useless if one does not reach water.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though applicable to anyone ignoring others’ needs, the verses were reportedly revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, who conditionally offered a Prophet follower money to return to Quraysh religion, then paid only part.
rows.anchor: these verses were reportedly revealed in relation to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, the verse asks whether the man who stopped giving charity knows his earlier deeds suffice or that his wealth will remain safe if he withholds charity.
rows.anchor: Does the one who stopped giving charity know that his past deeds will suffice or that his wealth will actually be preserved if he does not give it out in charity?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, it criticizes the arrogance of people acting as if they know better than God.
rows.anchor: In the broader Quranic context, it indicates the arrogance of those who act as if they know better than God; see 52:41; 68:47.

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Moses’ scriptures are named before Abraham’s despite chronology because they are more widely known.
rows.anchor: the scrolls of Moses are here mentioned before those of Abraham (v. 37), because they are more widely known (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham fulfilled by enduring trials none else endured, including being cast into the fire for breaking idols and agreeing to sacrifice his son before Gabriel stopped him.
rows.anchor: Abraham is referred to as he who fulfilled for patiently enduring what no one else was made to endure

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another view is that Abraham fulfilled the command to deliver God’s message.
rows.anchor: Others say this verse refers to Abraham’s fulfillment of the command to deliver God’s message (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A further view is that Abraham fulfilled his covenant with God.
rows.anchor: or to Abraham fulfilling the covenant with God (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As no one bears another’s sins, no one is rewarded for good deeds another person performed.
rows.anchor: Just as none will bear the sins of another, so too will none be rewarded for the good deeds performed by another.

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A famous hadith says a person’s deeds end at death except a righteous child’s supplication, continuing charity, and knowledge that benefits others.
rows.anchor: When a person dies, his deeds are cut off, save for three things: a righteous child who makes supplication for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everything done in life will be witnessed on Judgment Day; God judges deeds, people are shown them, and they testify to how they lived.
rows.anchor: This verse means that everything one does in this life will be witnessed on the Day of Judgment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is linked to 9:105, where the Prophet is told that God, the Messenger, and believers will see people’s deeds before their return to God for judgment.
rows.anchor: Thus the Prophet is told to say, Perform your deeds. God will see your deeds, as will the Messenger and the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Except verse 46, each verse in 42–50 begins wa anna, continuing the discussion of Moses’ and Abraham’s scriptures in 36–41.
rows.anchor: Each verse in this passage, except v. 46, begins with wa anna

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa anna may instead be read wa inna, making each instance an independent thought meaning truly, surely, or verily.
rows.anchor: But wa anna could also be read wa inna, which would make each occurrence mark a new, independent thought

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unto the Lord evokes Judgment Day, when everyone stands before God.
rows.anchor: Unto thy Lord conveys a sense of the Day of Judgment, when everyone will stand before God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although all created things ultimately return to God, different groups have different ends: the reverent are promised a Garden and disbelievers the Fire.
rows.anchor: there are nonetheless disparate ends for various groups, as in 13:35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverent laugh in the Hereafter and disbelievers weep, as described in 80:38–39.
rows.anchor: The reverent will thus be those who laugh, as in 80:38–39

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another understanding takes the ultimate end as a reference to God as the Necessary Being and Source of all beings.
rows.anchor: The ultimate end can also be seen as a reference to God as the One Necessary Being, Who is the Source of all beings (R).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: God decrees the causes of laughter and weeping and brings joy and sadness in this world.
rows.anchor: God decrees the causes that bring about laughter and weeping

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God makes believers laugh in the Garden and disbelievers weep in the Fire.
rows.anchor: God causes the believers to laugh in the Garden and the disbelievers to weep in the Fire

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: A further view is that believers laugh in the Hereafter and weep in this world, while disbelievers laugh in this world and weep in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: God causes the believers to laugh in the Hereafter and weep in this world

rows.speaker: Dhu’l-Nūn al-Miṣrī
rows.claim: He says knowledge of God makes the hearts of believers and gnostics laugh, while divine wrath and punishment darken the hearts of disbelievers and disobedient people.
rows.anchor: Dhu’l-Nūn al-Miṣrī is reported to have said, “He causes the hearts of the believers and the gnostics to laugh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s causing death and life demonstrates His power over every phase of existence and nonexistence.
rows.anchor: That it is He Who causes death and gives life

rows.speaker: ST
rows.claim: Another reading says God causes His enemies’ hearts to die through disbelief and gives His friends’ hearts life through faith and gnosis.
rows.anchor: He causes the hearts of His enemies to die

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two mates, male and female, are understood as created from a single soul.
rows.anchor: male and female—are said to be mates

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the second genesis as resurrection, with human creation from a drop demonstrating God’s ability to resurrect.
rows.anchor: resurrection is what is referred to here as the second genesis, according to most commentators

rows.speaker: Al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī takes the second genesis as the Spirit being breathed into a human, because the Spirit ennobles humans and distinguishes them from other animals.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī, however, understands the second genesis as a reference to the breathing of the Spirit into the human being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sirius is a first-magnitude star in Canis Major that pre-Islamic Arabs worshipped.
rows.anchor: Pre-Islamic Arabs worshipped Sirius (JJ), a star of the first magnitude belonging to Canis Major.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming God Lord of Sirius returns to 19–30’s theme that God alone rules what pagans attribute independent power to.
rows.anchor: This verse thus returns to the theme of vv. 19–30, emphasizing that God is the Lord of everything to which the pagans ascribe some independent power.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators classify the sūrah as Makkan; some classify verse 45 or verses 44–46 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: ost commentators maintain that al-Qamar is a Makkan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the moon mentioned in verse 1 and is also known by its opening words, Iqtarabat al-sāʿah.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of the moon in the first verse and is also known by its first words, Iqtarabat al-sāʿah

rows.speaker: Āl, Sy
rows.claim: The opening reiterates 53:57, and the destruction stories expand on the previous sūrah’s references to ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Noah.
rows.anchor: This sūrah follows thematically upon the previous sūrah in that the first verse reiterates 53:57, The imminent is nigh

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly recited Sūrah 50 and al-Qamar at both Eid prayers and other major prayer gatherings.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet would recite Qāf

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand the first two verses as the Prophet’s miracle: at Minā, after disbelievers demanded a sign, he pointed to the moon, which split in two around Mount Ḥirāʾ; he called them to witness and the division vanished.
rows.anchor: The first two verses of al-Qamar are understood by the vast majority of commentators as a reference to a miracle performed by the Prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents dismissed the split as sorcery, but one account says they decided to await travelers’ reports; travelers later confirmed seeing it too.
rows.anchor: According to one account, one of the disbelievers said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah warns the Prophet’s opponents of Judgment, recounts earlier peoples overthrown for similar offenses, then moves from punishment to divine decree and accounting and ends with the reverent’s reward.
rows.anchor: After warning the opponents of the Prophet of the judgment that will overtake them (vv. 1–8), the sūrah cites the people of Noah

none: translation only; verse text not recorded

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The Hour refers to the Final Hour and the world’s imminent demise.
rows.anchor: The Hour refers to the Final Hour as well as the imminent demise of the world (IK)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The Hour also refers to the Resurrection, as in verses 21:1 and 16:1.
rows.anchor: and to the Resurrection (JJ), as in 21:1: For mankind, their reckoning draws nigh, while they turn away heedless

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Hadith describe little time remaining between the Prophet’s coming and the world’s end relative to Earth’s lifespan; he illustrated this by pointing to his index and middle fingers.
rows.anchor: I was sent like this in relation to the Hour,” while pointing to his index finger and his middle finger

rows.speaker: a few commentators
rows.claim: A few commentators read the moon’s cleaving as a future end-time sign, though those who report this reading also mention the Prophet’s moon-splitting miracle.
rows.anchor: A few commentators note that the second half of this verse could be read, “and the moon will be cleaved,” referring to one of the signs of the end of time

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One interpretation takes man as a specific reference to the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Here man is understood by some as a specific reference to the Prophet Muhammad or to Adam (Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes man as a specific reference to Adam.
rows.anchor: Here man is understood by some as a specific reference to the Prophet Muhammad or to Adam (Q).

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators understand man to mean humanity as a whole.
rows.anchor: But most understand it as a reference to all of humanity.

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The sequence after God’s teaching of the Quran indicates that humans were made to know revelation before their creation in this world.
rows.anchor: The creation of human beings following directly upon the mention of God’s teaching the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pairing of humanity and revelation parallels 96:1–2, considered by most to be the first verses revealed chronologically.
rows.anchor: The correspondence between the mention of human beings and revelation here is similar to the combination mentioned in 96:1–2

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording subtly alludes to the mercy and blessing of creating humans and animals: womb, raḥim, shares root r-ḥ-m with the Compassionate, al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: the word for “womb,” raḥim, derives from the same root, r-ḥ-m, as the Compassionate, al-Raḥmān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A famous hadith has God tell the womb that He maintains relations with those who maintain kinship and severs relations with those who break it.
rows.anchor: I will keep good relations with one who keeps good relations with you
